articles.title: Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger review – mammoth tour movie brings the joy and poignancy of reunion
articles.summary: The Gallagher brothers’ comeback concerts are given the full fan-worship treatment, but it’s impossible to begrudge the euphoria they have created. “Hello … hello … It’s good to be back.” With these words – and the unfortunate possibility of a royalty payment to a certain disgraced ex-pop star …
body: Yet to the surprise of many who did not believe, and these biblical echoes are strangely appropriate, Liam and Noel did not fall out; the resulting stadium tour put a fresh coat of paint on the word “phenomenon”. Middle-aged and elderly people together with young people sporting bucket hats, some accompanied by their pets in bucket hats, sang their hearts out as if it was the 90s again and Manchester City had just won the World Cup 10-0 (although this film was evidently completed before Wonderwall’s moment at this year’s World Cup ).

As for the brothers’ togetherness, I think the film shows it is sincere and real in public, and real on stage, where it counts. Noel and Liam are rarely interviewed together; here mostly it is Noel solo. I wonder if, like Mick Jagger and Keith Richards, they now come together to make music after reaching an accommodation. Whatever wound each other up has not magically vanished, but is being managed. Part of the problem was that Noel’s songwriting credits made the big money – not Liam. Perhaps the lawyers have hammered something out here, but it is not shown in the film.

articles.title: ‘The Debut’ Explodes at Telluride With Julianne Moore’s Gonzo, Career-Best Turn, Thanks to a Toolbelt, Unlit Cigarettes and a Faux Musical
articles.summary: Jesse Eisenberg has made his most significant debut to date. There is a delicious irony at the center of “The Debut,” Eisenberg’s third feature as a director, which world premiered at the Telluride Film Festival: it is a film about a nobody who attacks a bit part as if it were the role of a
body: A24 sets it for Dec. 11, a release date that signals a studio going long — and A24 knows this walk. Twice it has turned an unlikely film into a best picture champion: “Moonlight,” which stunned the favored “La La Land and “Everything Everywhere All at Once,” an absurdist multiverse comedy that had no business winning and won anyway. “The Debut” hands the studio a broad, playable contender with two of the most beloved actors alive at its center.

Start with Moore, who has quietly become the film’s frontrunner-in-waiting. She is a five-time nominee with a single win — “Still Alice,” more than a decade ago — and Mona is the sort of tragicomic tour de force that reintroduces a great actor to voters who may have forgotten how much they owe her. She plays it balls to the wall, fearless in the way of Natalie Portman or Cate Blanchett at full tilt. On Telluride’s Saturday afternoon screening, she drew spontaneous applause in the middle of two separate scenes — the kind of response that tells you everything.

articles.title: Liam and Noel Gallagher Raise Fists and Electrify Venice as Oasis Doc Gets 8-Minute Standing Ovation
articles.summary: Oasis mania hit Venice Film Festival on Saturday night as Liam and Noel Gallagher presented the world premiere of their highly anticipated documentary “Don’t Look Back in Anger.” The rock doc received an eight-minute standing ovation as the once-estranged brothers held hands and raised them…
body: Directed by Dylan Southern and Will Lovelace, the documentary “charts Liam and Noel Gallagher’s triumphant reunion tour, Oasis Live ‘25, one of the most anticipated rock ‘n’ roll comebacks of our time,” according to its official synopsis. The film, which premieres in theaters Sept. 11 before bowing on Disney+ later this year, boasts footage of the band both backstage and onstage as well as the first joint interview with often-feuding brothers Noel and Liam in over 20 years.

The Oasis reunion tour last year marked the first time the Gallagher brothers had played together since 2009. Tickets for the tour sold out immediately and it went on to generate hundreds of millions of dollars across dates in the U.K., North America, South Korea, Japan, Australia, Argentina, Chile and Brazil.

articles.title: Three Films, and a Second Oscar? How Penélope Cruz Could Dominate Awards Season With ‘La Bola Negra,’ ‘The Invite’ and ‘Bunker’
articles.summary: Penélope Cruz became an Oscar winner when 2008’s “Vicky Cristina Barcelona” made her the first Spanish actress to win an acting Oscar. Seventeen years later, she is not chasing a second statuette so much as choosing which vehicle to ride to the ceremony — because this season she has three.
body: In Olivia Wilde’s A24 dinner-party comedy “The Invite,” which opened over the summer, she has another scene-stealing part opposite Edward Norton, a second potential route into the supporting actress race.
The genuinely unprecedented possibility is what happens if both supporting turns (and lead) catch fire — because this is the first season it even could.

Earlier this year, the Academy rewrote one of its oldest acting rules. Beginning with this year’s 99th Academy Awards, a performer can land two nominations in the same category, provided both performances finish among the top five in nominations voting. For decades, the lower vote-getter was simply erased. Now both can stand. Cruz is the marquee test case — Variety war-gamed this exact scenario when the rule changed.

It helps that all three films are already mounting serious campaigns of their own, quite apart from Cruz — buzz she can borrow without having to manufacture it, and dip into when she feels like it, not because she has to.

articles.title: Robert Pattinson says he had ‘twice as much time’ after birth of first child
articles.summary: Actor says of busy 2026 in which he has had several big roles: ‘Once you start spinning plates, it gets quite addictive’ Robert Pattinson has talked about the “addictive” nature of working on several films simultaneously, having starred in several of this year’s most highly anticipated productions…
body: “Once you get the momentum going, it’s strangely not that hard,” said Pattinson at the Venice film festival. “Once you start spinning plates, it gets quite addictive.”

The London-born performer has drawn critical praise this year for his turn as Antinous, the primary antagonist in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, as well as playing a lead role in the dark romantic comedy The Drama and making his Dune debut in the third instalment of the franchise this December.

On the Venice Lido, Pattinson was promoting Lance Oppenheim’s forthcoming arthouse thriller Primetime, which he joined as a producer before agreeing to star as the lead, and prepared while filming Lynne Ramsay’s Die My Love with Jennifer Lawrence.
“I just had a baby,” the actor told a press conference on the Lido. “So I had no desire to go out at night, so suddenly I had twice as much time to do anything with, which was very helpful.”

articles.title: ‘I don’t like the term neurodivergence – it sounds like political correctness’: Werner Herzog on fans, fanaticism and baby foxes
articles.summary: The Bavarian auteur talks directing Kate and Rooney Mara in Bucking Fastard and his popularity on Instagram. In outsider visionaries such as Aguirre, Fitzcarraldo or Timothy Treadwell, renegade German director Werner Herzog has created some of cinema’s most memorable monomaniacs – characters…
body: But suggestions that they could be role models for the modern-day neurodiversity movement send this famously fearless film-maker running for the hills. “I don’t like the term neurodivergence and ADHD, or whatever – it sounds like political correctness, which scares me under the table,” Herzog said at the Venice film festival.

The protagonist pair of Bucking Fastard, the new film that Herzog has brought to the Lido, slots right into his gallery of single-minded outsiders. Real-life sisters Kate and Rooney Mara play siblings Jean and Joan Holbrooke, who have separate bodies but speak in unison, dress the same and share the same preoccupations.

First they fall in love with their washed-up heart-throb neighbour (played by Orlando Bloom) and exact revenge when he marries another woman, then they embark on a quixotic quest to dig a tunnel connecting a cave in County Sligo to the Orkneys. Contemporary psychiatrists might detect behaviour consistent with autism or ADHD hyper-focus. Not Herzog.

articles.title: ‘The Row’ Review: ‘Icarus’ Director Bryan Fogel’s Doc Takes Viewers on a Gripping, Question-Raising Solo Voyage Across the Pacific
articles.summary: This Telluride-bowing film is a portrait of Tez Steinberg, who dealt with his grief by embarking on two massive long-distance solo rowing expeditions.
body: The Row, the new documentary from Bryan Fogel, does for open-sea rowing what the Oscar-winning Free Solo did for unassisted rock climbing, offering an intense yet meditative glimpse into the extremes people push themselves to in hopes of a catharsis that might have instead been achieved from a rigorous course of therapy.

It’s a gripping and moving documentary, but despite its attempted philosophical and nautical depth, it doesn’t benefit from post-screening contemplation. Unlike its protagonist, who’s constantly bursting through the limitations of human endurance — Fogel’s thematically complementary Icarus won the doc Oscar the year before Free Solo — the film has barriers it can’t quite seem to push past, despite some artistic adventurousness.

Fogel’s subject here is Tez Steinberg, a veteran of 47 marathons, two Iron Mans and one 145-mile ultra-marathon, who responded to his father’s death by deciding to row solo from California to Hawaii, a distance of 2,500 miles, in a 23-foot rowboat.

articles.title: Alan Hale Jr. Guest-Starred In A '60s Fantasy Series Featuring A Future Oscar Winner
articles.summary: TV used to be a wonderful, magical place where future Oscar-winner Sally Field could team up with Alan Hale Jr. in a show about a flying nun.
body: Like so many character actors of his era, Alan Hale Jr. spent much of the 1950s and '60s guest starring on classic Western TV shows. But the mid-20th Century didn't just give us a slew of small-screen oaters. It also gave us the fantasy sitcom, or "magi-com" — sitcoms where the "sit" in question involved some sort of fantastical character being introduced into an otherwise normal setting.

It started with the exploits of talking horse "Mister Ed," which gave rise to a host of similar shows including "I Dream of Jeannie," "My Living Doll," and of course "Bewitched." Hale Jr. even guest-starred on America's first fantasy sci-fi sitcom "My Favorite Martian." But that wasn't his only foray into the fantasy sitcom phenomenon. In 1969, three years after "Gilligan's Island" ended on CBS, Hale Jr. returned to the small screen in two episodes of the Sally Field-starring "The Flying Nun."

articles.title: Liam and Noel Gallagher Lock Arms at Venice Premiere of ‘Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger’
articles.summary: The two-hour documentary captures the brothers’ blockbuster Oasis Live ’25 reunion with intimate interviews and unprecedented access to rehearsals, backstage and stadium performances.
body: Today is gonna be the day — and maybe Liam and Noel Gallagher really are gonna live forever?

Further cementing their place in the pop cultural firmament, Manchester’s most cocksure duo walked the Venice Film Festival’s historic red carpet Saturday night for the world premiere of Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger, Disney’s much-anticipated behind-the-scenes documentary chronicling last year’s wildly successful globe-spanning reunion tour.

The premiere, appropriately, had more the feel of an Oasis stadium concert than a sombre festival premiere. There were chants of “Oasis! Oasis!” as the Gallaghers walked into the Sala Grande theater. Before the film, a fan in the balcony unveiled a banner with “Oasis Live 25 Buenos Aires” and chanted “Come on, Oasis!”
In response to a question yelled out from the gallery, Liam shouted out “Venice is a lovely place!” before sitting down with his brother to watch the film.

articles.title: Jeff Zucker on His Venice Film Festival Debut for A24’s ‘Primetime’: “This Is Very Surreal”
articles.summary: The former NBC Entertainment chief turned up on the Lido to support his film debut (playing himself!) opposite Robert Pattinson in Lance Oppenheim's dissection of 'To Catch a Predator.'
body: Standing near the entrance of Sala Grande on the Lido Saturday night, Jeff Zucker could almost pass for a typical Venice Film Festival attendee — almost.

Moments later something happens that shows just how atypical this attendee is: Venice Film Festival leadership, including artistic director Alberto Barbera, move in to approach and offer congratulations on his feature film debut and thank him for coming out to support the A24 release. Zucker is more than just a man about to sit for a movie on the festival’s most crowded night so far of the 83rd edition. He’s got a role in Oppenheim’s Primetime playing himself during his high-profile tenure running NBC Entertainment.
Zucker also couldn’t pass up the opportunity to come and support his big screen effort. “Life is crazy,” he told The Hollywood Reporter on the red carpet. “This is very surreal, but a lot of fun.”
